title: Children’s Place files for bankruptcy protection, seeks buyer
description: The Children's PlaceJames Leynse | Corbis | Getty ImagesChildren's clothing retailer The Children's Place has filed for chapter 11 bankruptcy protecti
body: The Children's PlaceJames Leynse | Corbis | Getty ImagesChildren's clothing retailer The Children's Place has filed for chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, it said Sunday.The company is looking to sell substantially all of its assets and is seeking offers from potential buyers by Dec. 9, with a goal to close a deal by the end of December. The retailer, whose brands include The Children's Place and Gymboree, says it operates two digital storefronts and 514 North American stores, and has distribution in 13 countries through franchise and wholesale partners. The company's performance has taken a hit in recent years from tariff hikes and slower consumer spending, among other factors.Its stores and e-commerce sites remain open for now, and the company is planning to continue its ongoing inventory sales with court approval. "For nearly 60 years, The Children's Place has supported growing families with apparel that customers have come to know and love. We recognize the significance of this development for our employees, customers, vendors, and other partners, and we are committed to conducting an efficient and transparent sale process," said Rudy Morando, co-chief restructuring officer of The Children's Place. "In the meantime, we remain focused on serving the families who have trusted The Children's Place for generations."This move comes days after interim Children's Place CEO Muhammad Asif Seemab and Chief Strategy Officer Muhammad Umair stepped down from their roles. Seemab and Umair will both remain on the company's board. CFO John Szczepanski took on the role of acting president and principal executive officer.Seemab is also managing director of Saudi-based Mithaq Capital, which took a majority stake in The Children's Place in 2024 when the company was facing financial trouble. Even with support from the investors, the company has not been able to significantly improve its financial outlook. In its bankruptcy filing, the company reported about $742 million in assets, compared to about $881 million in debts. In the second fiscal quarter of 2026, its most recently reported quarter, the company's net sales dropped nearly 19% from the same period the year prior. At the time, Seemab said in a news release that during the quarter the company was "stabilizing our customer file" and "driving traffic to our stores and websites," and saw "lower conversion, combined with a very clearance-heavy mix." He also pointed to tough comparisons to the prior-year period, due in part to back-to-school shopping demand that "was uniquely elevated ... ahead of anticipated tariff price increases."The Children's Place stock has plummeted in recent years and was trading around 18 cents per share on Monday.

schema.headline: Children’s Place files for bankruptcy protection, seeks buyer

title: PepsiCo to cut about 1,000 jobs as North American business struggles
description: Bottles of Pepsi are displayed in a store in New York City on March 17, 2025.Spencer Platt | Getty ImagesPepsiCo is cutting about 1,000 jobs across No
body: Bottles of Pepsi are displayed in a store in New York City on March 17, 2025.Spencer Platt | Getty ImagesPepsiCo is cutting about 1,000 jobs across North America as the company tries to turn around lagging sales in its home market."We have a clear ambition for PepsiCo North America: to build a stronger, more future-fit business that delivers industry-leading growth," Ram Krishnan, CEO of PepsiCo North America, wrote in a Monday letter to employees obtained by CNBC. "To do that, we need to be faster, more connected, and more capable, while continuing to invest in growth — behind our people, capabilities and brands."Over the next week, Pepsi plans to cut jobs as it says it aims to streamline its operations and better connect teams across the company's North American business. PepsiCo employs about 306,000 people worldwide, including roughly 125,000 in the United States, as of Dec. 27, according to a company filing. The Wall Street Journal first reported the coming layoffs.In October, PepsiCo cut its full-year earnings outlook, citing the struggles in its home market. During the third quarter, its North American beverage unit saw volume shrink 2%, while its North American food division reported flat volume. While the company has tried to boost sales by cutting prices and investing in marketing, the turnaround is taking longer than expected, Chief Financial Officer Steve Schmitt said on the company's earnings conference call.Shares of Pepsi rose slightly in afternoon trading. The stock is down nearly 1% this year, lagging behind the S&P 500's gains of nearly 11% over the same period.

schema.headline: PepsiCo to cut about 1,000 jobs as North American business struggles

title: Skydance outlines its $6 billion in planned cost savings. Here's the breakdown
description: David Ellison, co-chief executive officer of Skydance Corp., left, and Ynon Kreiz, co-chief executive officer of Skydance Corp., right, at the New Yor
body: David Ellison, co-chief executive officer of Skydance Corp., left, and Ynon Kreiz, co-chief executive officer of Skydance Corp., right, at the New York Stock Exchange, Oct. 8, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesSkydance is pulling back the curtain on how it plans to achieve at least $6 billion in cost savings in the next three years."By combining two global streaming services, two film and TV studio groups, two television portfolios, and overlapping corporate functions, we can reduce duplicative spend across an expense base of more than $50 billion," the company wrote in a letter to shareholders Monday as part of Paramount Skydance's third-quarter earnings release.Skydance, the company formed by the combination of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, said it projects at least $2.2 billion in cost reductions from eliminating "redundant back-office and corporate functions," including eliminating management layers and ramping the use of artificial intelligence. Those savings also account for "rationalizing" its office footprint. Skydance expects at least $1 billion in savings from streamlining marketing and promotional spending. And around $1.4 billion in savings will come from unifying its streaming businesses and broadcast architecture and integrating back-end technology. A final $1.4 billion in savings will be tied to "optimizing third-party spend," eliminating overlapping expenses, and consolidating purchasing decisions to one centralized group, Skydance said."We are confident in achieving these savings, drawing on our playbook from Paramount," the company wrote. "That program is on track to achieve over $2.7 billion in run-rate efficiencies by the end of 2026."Some of that cost-cutting has already begun. Last month, Skydance began offering voluntary buyouts to employees ahead of official layoffs. At the same time, the company adopted a five-day-per-week in-office policy. Additionally, last week saw the departure of eight executives — four from Warner Bros. and four from Paramount.The company has previously said it plans to eventually merge the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services into a single platform. On Monday, Skydance said it would take the first step toward that goal early next year, offering a bundle of the streaming services "at an even greater value."Co-CEO Ynon Kreiz told investors during the company's earnings call that Skydance is also looking for ways to optimize its content budget. The company spends more than $30 billion annually on shows and films. "As one company, we can make smarter choices about how we distribute and monetize both new content and library content," Kreiz said.Skydance noted that it's expecting a $200 million headwind in the fourth quarter from theatrical underperformances at Warner Bros. studio related to already launched titles and upcoming releases.The company will also utilize AI to speed up production and decrease costs to make films, co-CEO and chairman David Ellison said on the call."We think these tools will help unlock more original storytelling by being able to make the budget more digestible to be able to take that amount of risk," Ellison said.The updates came alongside third-quarter results for the legacy Paramount Skydance company that included revenue of $7.03 billion, which was roughly in line with StreetAccount estimates of $7.04 billion, and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $1 billion, topping StreetAccount estimates of $913.5 million. However, adjusted earnings per share of 45 cents were not immediately comparable to StreetAccount EPS estimates. The results don't include the impact of the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, which closed after the end of the third quarter. Skydance detailed business units of the combined entity, including studios, direct-to-consumer and TV, and said it will provide full-year guidance during its fourth-quarter earnings report early next year. "Going forward, we will provide guidance on an annual basis, as we prioritize long-term value creation, which we believe will be more consistent with our strategic approach," the company told shareholders. "We will continue to provide quarterly updates, including certain forward-looking commentary where applicable, which will give investors visibility into our near-term progress of the business."

schema.headline: Skydance outlines its $6 billion in planned cost savings. Here's the breakdown

title: Trump questions midterm election results, revives voting-machine conspiracy
description: US President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office of the White House, Washington, DC, on Nov. 5, 2026. Mandel Ngan | AFP | Getty ImagesPresident Don
body: US President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office of the White House, Washington, DC, on Nov. 5, 2026. Mandel Ngan | AFP | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Monday questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results, resurrecting his pattern of raising doubts about electoral losses for himself and other Republicans.Trump's social media post raising questions about the election came six days after his fellow Republicans suffered historic defeats at the polls nationwide, including in several GOP strongholds like Texas and South Carolina."Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest," Trump wrote on Truth Social."How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting 'dumps' were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote," the president said. "It's all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!"Trump's post was a sharp pivot from what has been a conciliatory tone after last Tuesday's thumping of Republican candidates, which resulted in Democrats regaining majorities in both the Senate and House of Representatives.On Election Night, Trump told The New York Times that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results of the midterms, and that he was willing to work with Democrats."We'll, you know, look forward to working with them," Trump told The Times. "We'll probably work something out."The next day, Trump said, "I'll get along probably with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive."Later in the week, he announced he was replacing White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with her deputy, Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration's aggressive immigration enforcement crackdown, which has drawn widespread criticism from Democrats.Sen. Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who could be the majority leader in the Senate in January, said in a post on X, "Donald Trump's pathetic return to election denialism was inevitable.""He can whine all he wants, but nothing will stop this inescapable truth: For the last two years of his presidency, Trump will face the largest Democratic congressional majorities in decades, all because he has been an unprecedented failure," Schumer said.After his electoral loss to former President Joe Biden in 2020, Trump argued, without evidence, that he only lost as a result of widespread ballot fraud.Trump's claims, which were joined by dozens of unsuccessful court cases challenging election procedures, culminated in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol by a mob of his supporters after he spoke at a rally outside the White House.The riot disrupted a joint session of Congress for hours. Later that day, Congress confirmed Biden's election by the Electoral College.Critics of Trump's conspiracy theories about elections have noted that he lost the 2020 race when he was president, but won the 2024 presidential election, when Biden was in the White House. They also noted that in the past week, Republicans had control of states that saw major Democratic wins that few analysts would have predicted a year ago, including Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, and Iowa.

schema.headline: Trump questions midterm election results, revives voting-machine conspiracy

title: Millions of dollars poured into prediction markets on election night, trading on Democratic control of Congress and Texas governor's race
description: The Kalshi 2026 midterm election prediction website arranged on a laptop in Forest Hills, New York, Oct. 28, 2026.Gabby Jones | Bloomberg | Getty Imag
body: The Kalshi 2026 midterm election prediction website arranged on a laptop in Forest Hills, New York, Oct. 28, 2026.Gabby Jones | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMore than 87% of all election markets across Kalshi and Polymarket gave the right candidate at least a 90% chance of winning their race 24 hours before election night, a CNBC analysis found.Election night showed how traders reacted to real-time midterm results, as trading activity surged and market prices shifted to Democrats after results from Indiana began rolling in before 7 p.m. on Nov. 3. Many midterm races were uncompetitive, which boosted the overall hit rate on prediction markets."I'd say prediction markets did pretty well," said Koleman Strumpf, a professor of economics at Wake Forest University. "But they didn't outperform the best," he added, referring to traditional forecast polls that tracked results that night. Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.Prediction markets saw big trades on election night. After 8 p.m. on Nov. 3, at least $1 million was traded on a Kalshi market that incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott would be reelected. Abbott eventually lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa by more than 700,000 votes, according to the Associated Press. A little after 11 p.m. on election night, more than $1.4 million was traded on Kalshi that Republicans would not secure control of the House of Representatives.Following the midterms, both Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan and Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour were on the social media platform X crediting prediction markets for correctly predicting races. Nate Silver, a political forecaster and founder of the Silver Bulletin newsletter, disputed the claim, arguing forecast models influenced prediction market movement. Silver joined Polymarket as an advisor in 2024.  "Prediction market probabilities strongly converged toward [our models] in individual Senate and gubernatorial races," Silver wrote on Silver Bulletin. "I was tracking this stuff closely, precisely because I envisioned that we might wind up in this sort of debate where prediction markets are low-key stealing valor from the models."Sports still dominatePrediction market volume on midterm election-related contracts across Kalshi and Polymarket more than tripled from the last week of October into the midterms week, according to a CNBC analysis of data published on Predictions.com. The data did not include combo markets, which bundle multiple contracts and pay out only if every leg resolves in the trader's favor.Still, volume on midterm contracts pales in comparison with sports volume, which remains larger than all other categories. Kalshi exceeded $3 billion in total midterm contract volume, according to the platform's website, which also includes volume for contracts on mayoral races. Last week, Polymarket's two exchanges reported nearly $700 million in volume for midterm contracts. While prediction markets broadly anticipated Democratic control of Congress, the blue tsunami is expected to bite the industry in other ways. Three days after the midterms, Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif, criticized the federal regulator responsible for the platforms, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, for allowing sports contracts."Sports prediction markets are sports bets. By effectively requiring prediction markets to offer contracts in all 50 states, even on Tribal lands, the CFTC is once again violating state law and Tribal sovereignty," Schiff wrote on X. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Millions of dollars poured into prediction markets on election night, trading on Democratic control of Congress and Texas governor's race

title: Home listings pile up in October, but sellers won't slash prices
description: Homes in San Francisco, California, US, on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesHomebuyers continue to retreat, but sel
body: Homes in San Francisco, California, US, on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesHomebuyers continue to retreat, but sellers are still digging in, refusing to cut prices or give up. As a result, September's frozen housing market is now October's frozen and increasingly bloated market.Active inventory in October hit 183,500 homes, up 7.4% year-over-year, according to Realtor.com. That is the fastest annual growth in eight months. Active listings have been rising each month since February. This is despite the fact that new listings are actually falling, down 7.5% from October 2025.The market has seen several years of extremely lean supply, driven by the homebuying frenzy during the first two years of the pandemic, when mortgage rates hit more than a dozen record lows. Now supply nationally is just 6.6% below typical pre-pandemic levels, the narrowest gap since the pandemic."The market is cooling on both sides, but in different ways. Buyers are stepping back as higher mortgage rates cut into their buying power, while sellers are listing less often without a broad increase in delistings or price cuts," said Danielle Hale, chief economist at Realtor.com. "We're seeing a pause in new supply, but owners who already have homes on the market appear to be largely unphased."Just over 20% of sellers cut prices in October, about the same as both September and October of last year. There was also no meaningful increase in delistings by sellers.Mortgage rates came down a little bit in October month-to-month, but they are still over a full percentage point higher than a year ago. That continued to weigh on sales. Newly pending sales, representing signed contracts, not closings, dropped 16.8% in October year-over-year, according to Zillow. That was the biggest annual drop since August 2023 and slowest October since 2018.  While rates fell slightly, home prices continued to gain. Zillow estimated the monthly mortgage payment on the typical U.S. home was $2,004 in October, assuming a 20% down payment and excluding taxes and insurance. That is an increase of 12.8% from last year and 4.8% higher than in September, the biggest one-month jump in four years. "November is shaping up to have an even larger contraction, but the silver lining is that next month is likely going to be the worst of it," said Mischa Fisher, Zillow's chief economist, in a release. "I expect the pace of the slowdown to ease into the new year. There are deals to be had for buyers able to brave the affordability headwinds in the coming months, and the continued inventory buildup means there is a lot of upside for sales into next year if we get rate relief."Get Property Play directly to your inboxCNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.Subscribe here to get access today.

schema.headline: Home listings pile up in October, but sellers won't slash prices

title: Honda to invest $3 billion in new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio
description: A Honda sedan moves down the assembly line on Jan. 28, 2025 at the automaker's assembly plant in Marysville, Ohio. Michael Wayland / CNBCMARYSVILLE, O
body: A Honda sedan moves down the assembly line on Jan. 28, 2025 at the automaker's assembly plant in Marysville, Ohio. Michael Wayland / CNBCMARYSVILLE, Ohio — Honda Motor plans to invest $3 billion to build a new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio, the automaker announced Monday.Honda said the new plant, which will be near its other facilities in Marysville, Ohio, is expected to begin production in 2029, have a capacity for 240,000 vehicles annually and create more than 2,000 jobs. The facility is expected to be capable of producing traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines, all-electric vehicles and hybrid models, which have been growing in popularity in the U.S. Honda declined to disclose what vehicles the company plans to produce at the new facility.The plant is expected to increase Honda's light-duty vehicle capacity to 1.3 million units annually in the U.S. It currently has 12 manufacturing plants in United States, eight of which produce engines or light-duty vehicles for the auto industry. "This is not simply an investment in another plant. It is an investment in the future of Honda manufacturing in America," Bob Nelson, executive vice president of American Honda Motor, said during the announcement at the company's U.S. heritage center in Ohio.The auto industry has been trying to localize more production amid President Donald Trump's tariffs and inflated logistics costs that have cut into profits.Nelson told CNBC after the event that tariffs are affecting the company's business but the new plant is more about Honda's ambitions to grow in the U.S."Tariffs are an impact to us, even with the high localization rate that we have," he said. "But the real impact is that we have customers out there wanting Honda product and we can't give it to them. That's the real area."Nelson said Honda did not work with the Trump administration ahead of Monday's announcement.Honda's plans for a new plant come roughly two weeks after Volkswagen-owned luxury brand Audi announced it would invest more than $4 billion in a new plant at a rally with President Donald Trump, which Audi CEO Gernot Dollner faced criticism for attending.Honda's new plant is the company's first new mass production U.S. vehicle assembly plant since it opened a facility in Indiana in 2008. It also opened a $70 million performance vehicle facility in 2016 and a multibillion-dollar joint venture battery plant earlier this year, both in Ohio.The announcement comes after the automaker in May indefinitely suspended an $11 billion investment plan to produce all-electric vehicles and batteries in Canada. It also canceled three planned EVs for the U.S. market.American Honda Motor Co. executive Jennifer Thomas recently emphasized the Japanese automaker's commitment to the U.S. and need for additional capacity."In order to be competitive in this market, you're going to need to build products here," Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs, said Oct. 27 in Detroit. "We are focused on trying to maximize the existing capacity that we have, but we are at capacity, and so we're exploring all options."Thomas also warned the automotive industry faces a "catastrophic" scenario if the U.S. and Canada cannot reach a new trade deal by the end of this year, when Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries don't reach a deal.Honda said it has built more than 33 million vehicles and more than 39 million engines in the U.S. since it started auto production in the U.S. in 1982.The Japanese automaker currently has more than 30,000 employees in the U.S.

schema.headline: Honda to invest $3 billion in new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio

title: SoftBank Group shares surge 13% as Asian tech stocks track Wall Street rebound
description: CANADA - 2025/08/07: In this photo illustration, the SoftBank Group (Soft Bank) logo is seen displayed on a smartphone screen. (Photo Illustration by
body: CANADA - 2025/08/07: In this photo illustration, the SoftBank Group (Soft Bank) logo is seen displayed on a smartphone screen. (Photo Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesAsian technology stocks surged Tuesday, tracking a rebound on Wall Street overnight as a sharp decline in oil prices lifted sentiment while renewed buying in chip names spilled over into Asia, following last week's bruising sell-off.Japan's technology investment giant SoftBank Group surged 13.4%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest gained 2.36%. Semiconductor equipment maker Tokyo Electron rose over 4.73%, while Lasertec and Disco advanced 6.74% and 6.01%, respectively.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconStock performance so far this yearSouth Korean chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 5.2%, while Samsung Electronics rose 3.9%. Samsung SDI climbed 6.87%. Taiwan's TSMC added 0.45%.China's tech-heavy ChiNext Price Index rose 1.4%.The gains followed a strong session on Wall Street, where the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.74%, while the S&P 500 rose 2.35% to clock its best day since April 8.The recovery came after a steep sell-off in global technology stocks last week, fueled by concerns that Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-center development, potentially impacting demand for artificial intelligence chips and infrastructure."This is not to suggest that the tech sell-off is done and dusted. While there is some evidence that investors are taking advantage of last week's plunge to increase their exposure to chip and other AI-adjacent stocks, there's a danger that it may be a little bit premature to load up and 'buy the dip,'" said David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation.Beyond the political uncertainty surrounding potential restrictions on data-center development, investors have also grown increasingly wary of the enormous capital expenditures required to build out AI infrastructure. Questions over how quickly those investments will translate into meaningful profits have weighed on sentiment toward companies across the semiconductor supply chain.

schema.headline: SoftBank Group shares surge 13% as Asian tech stocks track Wall Street rebound

title: Jensen Huang exit odds are low on prediction markets after Nvidia probe
description: Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., during the launch of the Sferical One AI supercomputer in Stockholm, Sweden, on Thursday, Oct.
body: Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., during the launch of the Sferical One AI supercomputer in Stockholm, Sweden, on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. Erik Flyg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNvidia's board is investigating CEO Jensen Huang, citing recent reports that he's been targeted by a "foreign intelligence effort," but traders on prediction markets think it's unlikely he'll be ousted as chief.On Sunday, Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials  —  according to The New York Times – say is a spy for China's Ministry of State Security.On Kalshi, speculators say there's just a 17% chance Huang is gone by 2027. Those odds rise to 30% by 2028, and 35% by 2029. However, they think there is a 75% probability that Huang will depart by 2031. Contracts on Huang's departure on Kalshi are resolved using information from Bloomberg.On Polymarket, speculators place just one-in-four odds that Huang resigns or is forced out by the end of March 2027. Contracts are resolved on the platform using official statements from the company or Huang himself. Shares of Nvidia were down more than 5% after the news on Monday.Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Jensen Huang exit odds are low on prediction markets after Nvidia probe

title: Hegseth impeachment articles introduced by Rep. Massie
description: Pete Hegseth, U.S. secretary of defense, during a roundtable in the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 21, 2026.Aaron Schwartz
body: Pete Hegseth, U.S. secretary of defense, during a roundtable in the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 21, 2026.Aaron Schwartz | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesRep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., on Monday introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, triggering a vote in the House of Representatives as early as this week. The unusual impeachment push against Hegseth by a member of his own party comes after Democrats swept to majorities in both the House and Senate during last week's midterm elections. Many Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have cited the Iran war Hegseth has led as a reason for the electoral bludgeoning. Massie, who lost his reelection bid in a Republican primary in May, introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth. They include waging war in contravention of war powers resolutions Congress passed to limit war, extrajudicial killings tied to boat strikes in the Caribbean that purported to target drug smugglers and suppressing free speech by targeting Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a veteran. "Wherefore, Secretary of Defense Peter Hegseth, by such conduct, has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law," the articles, which Massie read from the House floor, read. "Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office, and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States."Massie's resolution will force House Republican leaders to put the measure up for a vote by the end of this week. Impeachment resolutions are privileged, meaning the House must act on them, table them or vote to refer them to committee within two legislative days. President Donald Trump once again defended Hegseth later Monday, telling reporters at the White House he will stand by the secretary even if he is impeached."He won two wars. He was in charge," said Trump, who was impeached twice in his first presidential term.Trump also credited Hegseth with boosting military recruitment, claiming there are "waiting lists of people trying to get in.""He's done a very good job," Trump said.U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) holds a press conference about his resolution to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., Nov. 9, 2026.Evelyn Hockstein | ReutersCongress has the authority to impeach Cabinet secretaries, though it is a highly unusual move. Republican leadership in the House has not yet laid out how they plan to deal with the Hegseth impeachment, and it is unclear whether they have the votes to dispose of Massie's measure following the election. The last Cabinet Secretary to be impeached was Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024 over his handling of the U.S.-Mexico border. Before Mayorkas, a Cabinet secretary had not been impeached since Secretary of War William Belknap in 1876. Neither was convicted by the Senate.If the House votes to impeach Hegseth, the Senate would be tasked with holding a trial and voting on removing the secretary from office. If convicted by a two-thirds majority of the Senate, Hegseth would be removed from office. Republicans hold a razor-thin 218-214 majority in the House, meaning only a handful of Republican defections could result in Hegseth's impeachment. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., reiterated his support for impeaching Hegseth on Monday at his first press conference at the Capitol since last Tuesday's elections. "Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America's national security, and he's the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran," Jeffries said.Hegseth has appeared to be preparing for an impeachment fight. The secretary put out a video last week defending his actions atop the Pentagon, and the department has led a media campaign to "Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic." Hegseth on Monday announced he would hold a press conference Tuesday morning at the Pentagon. His most recent press conference way May 5, just over two months after the Iran war began.

schema.headline: Hegseth impeachment articles introduced by Rep. Massie

title: Lucid misses Wall Street’s earnings expectations, expands loan from Saudi Arabia fund
description: The Lucid Motors Lucid Air electric car at the 91st edition of the International Paris Motor Show at the Porte de Versailles in Paris, Oct. 12, 2026.L
body: The Lucid Motors Lucid Air electric car at the 91st edition of the International Paris Motor Show at the Porte de Versailles in Paris, Oct. 12, 2026.Ludovic Marin | AFP | Getty ImagesLucid Group missed Wall Street's third-quarter expectations as the embattled electric vehicle maker continues an "operational reset" aimed at cutting costs and narrowing losses.The company on Monday also announced a $1.75 billion increase in a delayed draw term loan from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the company's largest shareholder.Lucid stock fell roughly 5% in aftermarket trading Monday.Here's how Lucid performed in the third quarter compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:Loss per share: $2.74 vs. a loss of $2.28 expectedRevenue: $350 million vs. $407 million expectedDespite the top- and bottom-line misses, the company's adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of a loss of $726 million beat Wall Street's expectations of a loss of $611 million for the third quarter. Its net loss for the quarter was $830.9 million, down from a loss of $978.4 million a year earlier.Lucid's 2025 third quarter included revenue of $336.6 million, a loss of $3.31 per share and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $717.7 million.The quarterly results are the first since Lucid CEO Silvio Napoli, who started leading the company in June, announced a restructuring plan that included implementing several cost-cutting efforts and delaying the company's upcoming midsize vehicle from the end of this year until the second half of next."Our transformation is beginning to show progress. We are acting with urgency, strengthening the fundamentals and driving greater discipline, while continuing to invest in the priorities to deliver profitable long-term growth," Napoli said in a release.The company's turnaround plan includes $1.4 billion in cash flow improvements this year as well as focusing attention on a robotaxi program with Uber and Nuro, a factory that's under construction in Saudi Arabia and the midsize vehicle.Lucid said the capital from PIF is expected to give the company "additional financial flexibility as Lucid delivers on its turnaround program." It is expected to assist in funding "operations and key investments" into the fourth quarter of 2027, including the start of production for the midsize vehicle.The additional funds boost Lucid's total liquidity to $3.75 billion, up from $2 billion to end the third quarter."We are grateful for the continued financial support from our anchor shareholder, which further energizes us to remain focused on execution and on our commitments as we build a stronger, sustainable Lucid," Napoli said.Lucid said Monday that the company expects to communicate its midterm plan and targets early next year. The EV maker in May suspended its guidance and many targets, citing new leadership and time needed to develop a turnaround plan.

schema.headline: Lucid misses Wall Street’s earnings expectations, expands loan from Saudi Arabia fund

title: Trump sees 'strong inclination' to end Russia-Ukraine war ahead of U.S.-brokered peace talks
description: US President Donald Trump during a news conference in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Monday, Nov.
body: US President Donald Trump during a news conference in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. Trump said the FBI is looking into Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang's affair with a woman who is reportedly suspected to have been a Chinese intelligence officer. Photographer: Tierney L. Cross/The Washington Post/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesBloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump said Washington sees growing willingness to end Russia's war in Ukraine, as Kyiv and Moscow prepare for U.S.-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi later Tuesday.Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said recent battlefield gains were strengthening Kyiv's negotiating position ahead of the talks.Speaking to reporters at the White House on Monday, Trump said both sides were battle-weary, more than four and a half years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022."We're also seeing a very strong inclination to end Russia and Ukraine," Trump said, adding that, "We're involved in that because I want to see people stop getting killed again."His comments followed a U.S. official’s assessment that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing some flexibility over a possible exchange of territory, according to Reuters.A senior Ukrainian official, however, rejected suggestions that Kyiv was considering territorial concessions, telling Reuters that any discussion of territory would have to take place between national leaders and be accompanied by appropriate security guarantees.Russia has publicly maintained its demand that Ukraine surrender the entire eastern Donbas region, including territory Moscow has not captured.Separately, Zelenskyy said Monday that recent Ukrainian battlefield gains and mounting Russian losses had improved Kyiv's bargaining power."Right now, Ukrainian troops are truly strengthening Ukraine's negotiating positions," he said in his nightly address, urging Washington to convince Russia to end the war.The remarks come as U.S., Russian and Ukrainian officials prepare for two days of talks in Abu Dhabi — their first trilateral negotiations since February. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are set to lead Washington’s mediation efforts, with postwar security guarantees for Ukraine expected to feature prominently.Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that discussions had advanced on a possible postwar security framework for Ukraine and Europe."Nothing's been finalized yet, and maybe some progress can be made in Abu Dhabi," Rubio said.The renewed diplomacy comes amid continued fighting and mounting questions over the scale of Russia's wartime losses.Belarusian Cyber Partisans, an opposition-linked hacker group, said its analysis of data it claims was obtained from Russia's state statistics agency identified 393,881 deaths linked to military operations or their consequences between 2022 and August 2026. The group said its count was based on death records explicitly coded as resulting from hostilities or their consequences. It acknowledged that the figure could include civilians and deaths connected to other conflicts, while excluding personnel who are missing but have not been declared dead.Rosstat has acknowledged that it was targeted in cyberattacks but denied that its databases were compromised, according to a Russian media outlet Kommersant. The hackers' claims and the underlying dataset have not been independently verified in full.Separately, the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that 400,000 to 450,000 Russian military personnel were killed between February 2022 and June 2026. At the upper end, that would be more than nine times the combined Soviet and Russian military fatalities in wars since World War II, according to the think tank.The Moscow Times, citing a broader analysis of the leaked records, reported that roughly 450,000 war-related deaths would make the conflict Russia's fourth most common cause of death since 2022. The newspaper said it had cross-checked a sample of names, but could not verify the data set in its entirety.

schema.headline: Trump sees 'strong inclination' to end Russia-Ukraine war ahead of U.S.-brokered peace talks

title: Boeing to cut 5% of commercial airplane workers as production increase takes longer than expected
description: Boeing Co. 737 Max airplanes at the company's manufacturing facility in Renton, Washington, US, on Wednesday, April 15, 2026. M. Scott Brauer | Bloomb
body: Boeing Co. 737 Max airplanes at the company's manufacturing facility in Renton, Washington, US, on Wednesday, April 15, 2026. M. Scott Brauer | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBoeing said Monday that it plans to cut 5% of its commercial airplane workforce as its production ramp-up is moving at a slower pace than the company expected.The cuts will be through a combination of attrition and layoffs, Stephanie Pope, head of the commercial aircraft unit, said in a memo to staff.Pope reiterated that the company is still working to stabilize production rates of its bestselling 737 Max planes, which are made outside of Seattle.CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors last month that the company won't significantly increase production of the Max aircraft until the second half of next year. He said the company's wing production has been slower than expected."Adjusting our production schedules and reducing aircraft output puts us in an overstaffed position," Pope said in her note Monday. "Unfortunately, that means we need to align our staffing levels to our revised business plan, resulting in a reduction of approximately 5% through a combination of attrition and involuntary layoffs, with notifications beginning in December." Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. Ortberg said the company has been trying to stabilize output at a rate of about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.

schema.headline: Boeing to cut 5% of commercial airplane workers as production increase takes longer than expected

title: 3 unexpected reasons the October jobs report was so strong
description: FG Construction displays a We're Hiring! sign during the Mega JobNewsUSA South Florida Job Fair held in the Amerant Bank Arena on April 30, 2026 in Su
body: FG Construction displays a We're Hiring! sign during the Mega JobNewsUSA South Florida Job Fair held in the Amerant Bank Arena on April 30, 2026 in Sunrise, Florida. Joe Raedle | Getty ImagesA little-noticed category in Friday's blockbuster jobs report is challenging the consensus view about job losses caused by artificial intelligence.At least for now, the data suggests the U.S. is gaining jobs as a result of the AI boom, not losing them.And another category suggests the strong jobs numbers could have some staying power.Nonfarm payrolls grew by 165,000 jobs in October, according to the Friday report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It was a surprising surge in hiring that blew way past Wall Street's expectations. Economists polled by Dow Jones had forecast growth of just 59,000 for the month.Here are three surprising things you might have missed from the report.ConsultingHiring for consultants surged in the month, sending the profession's total head count to a fresh record.The labor force for management, scientific and technical consultants expanded by 17,300 jobs between September and October, the largest month-over-month increase in nearly two years. This category is a subset of the professional and business services sector tracked by BLS and accounted for 25% of the entire sector's gains for the month.What's more, this workforce has grown by more than 45,000 jobs over the past year. That gain pushed the total employee base for these types of workers past 1.9 million for the first time on record, according to BLS data.Hiring in the industry had largely stalled since 2023 following years of rapid expansion during the pandemic. Wall Street has questioned if the rise of artificial intelligence will curb demand for these services. Those fears have led shares of consulting firm Gartner to lose more than half of their value over the past three years. Accenture and FTI Consulting have dropped about 18% and 9% over that period, even as the S&P 500 has climbed roughly 74%. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconGartner vs the S&P 500 over the last 5 yearsNow, some economists are speculating that the recent jump could be driven by businesses hiring consultants to help them adopt AI. Gartner forecast in September that worldwide AI spending would total $2.7 trillion in 2026, a nearly 50% increase year over year."The AI buildout and corporate interests to increase utilization will keep the technical consultants employed," said Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial.Roach called the consulting sector a bright spot in October that is "worth watching." He noted that these jobs also saw double-digit growth in the late 1990s, as firms raced to implement new internet technology into their businesses.So far, data suggests that AI may be adding more jobs to the labor market than it is taking away through automation. An assessment by Moody's Analytics found that AI has created a net 786,000 jobs since ChatGPT launched in November 2022, driven in part by data center construction."Wasn't AI supposed to destroy jobs? The most dystopian scenarios even called for mass unemployment," Mark Zandi, Moody's chief economist, wrote in a social media post on Monday. "That risk hasn't gone away, and AI-driven productivity gains could still shift into a higher gear. But for now, AI is adding to job growth, not subtracting from it."Temporary hiresHiring of temporary workers also drove growth, which could signal that the labor market is heating up.The subsector's payrolls grew by 18,600 in October, one of its largest month-over-month increases since 2022. This category is another part of the professional and business services sector and accounted for 27% of the sector's gains for the month.The total size of this workforce is still well below record highs set in 2022. But headcount has grown roughly 3% since December and now sits at levels last seen in April 2025, the month that President Donald Trump's rollout of his plan for steep tariffs put corporate America on alert.Economists see temporary hiring as a leading indicator in the labor market. Conventional wisdom suggests that companies that hire new workers on a short-term basis often transition them to full-time roles later.That could be what's happening here, but the fact that the end of the year is approaching makes it harder to tell. The boost could be a result of hiring as the holiday shopping season approaches — and if employers are staffing up for the holidays, they are less likely to retain those workers when January rolls around. Such hiring hasn't typically happened this early, but the season creeps earlier each year. The BLS adjusts its numbers to account for seasonal trends, but won't immediately make an adjustment if the trend is changing. One hint that holiday hiring may be shifting comes in a separate category of workers: couriers and messengers. This is another area that acts as a barometer for holiday labor demand, and just over one out of every 10 new jobs in the month was in this category.That category "bears watching for reversal in the months ahead," said Jason Pride, chief of investment strategy and research at Glenmede, a wealth manager.Election spendingHiring related to political campaigns in the final weeks of an expensive election cycle could have also boosted payrolls.Employment in political organizations has historically spiked heading into midterm or presidential elections, according to a BLS analysis. Staffing levels tend to peak in October of those years, the data shows. Nonfarm payrolls expanded in the months before the 2018 and 2022 midterm elections.But the vast size of campaign coffers this cycle may have translated into more jobs than before. The 2026 congressional election is slated to go down in history as the most expensive midterm on record, according to an analysis from OpenSecrets, a money-in-politics watchdog group. Billions of dollars spent on campaigns may have translated into paid gigs that involve door knocking, phone banking or other election-related work.

schema.headline: 3 unexpected reasons the October jobs report was so strong

title: Elizabeth Warren set to take over the Senate banking committee. Here's what she plans to do
description: Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) campaigns with Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed at Eastern Michigan University on Nov. 2, 2026,
body: Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) campaigns with Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed at Eastern Michigan University on Nov. 2, 2026, in Ypsilanti, Michigan.Salwan Georges | Getty ImagesSen. Elizabeth Warren is set to take over the Senate Banking Committee. The Massachusetts Democrat is already charting the panel's course.Among Warren's top issues for the Congress that convenes in January are addressing the cost of living, tightening export controls on advanced artificial intelligence chips to China and promulgating regulations for prediction markets, according to a Warren banking committee aide. The aide spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the yet-to-be-announced agenda. Warren is also plotting an aggressive oversight agenda and urged tech CEOs, administration officials and Wall Street executives to preserve their documents, the aide said. Democrats' dominant win in last week's midterm elections hands them control of committee gavels on Capitol Hill. With that comes the ability to set the legislative agenda for the House and Senate and subpoena power to compel government officials and business leaders to testify under oath. The Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee has a broad remit, including jurisdiction over federal monetary policy, banks and export controls.Warren's plans to tackle affordability include capping credit card interest rates, following up her 21st Century Road to Housing Act with additional legislation to build more affordable homes and lowering medical, consumer and student debt. The aide said Warren also intends to put constraints on AI chips going to China, while shaping rules for AI at home. Warren is also seeking to end the "Wild West-style" lack of oversight in the prediction market industry, the aide said. She and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis have already written to Kalshi and Polymarket demanding information on safeguards around election-related markets. The banking committee is also likely to be at the center of Democrats' oversight agenda, which is expected to cast a wide net into private industry. Warren said tech CEOs, administration officials, Trump family cryptocurrency businesses and Wall Street executives should prepare to answer the committee's questions and should preserve their documents, the aide said.

schema.headline: Elizabeth Warren set to take over the Senate banking committee. Here's what she plans to do
